title: OpenAI Agrees Not to Use Disputed Apple Hardware Trade Secrets
summary:
The developer of the ChatGPT AI assistant will provide forensic images of 14 employees' devices and allow court access to its recruitment records to avoid the destruction of evidence. OpenAI also agreed to stop using intellectual property it is accused of stealing from Apple in an ongoing hardware trade secrets suit, after US District Judge Edward Davila indicated a preliminary injunction against the AI firm is likely. Judge Davila ordered OpenAI to produce interview materials for former Apple hardware hires within 14 days to determine if candidates were asked to share prototype details.

OpenAI countered the suit by alleging a former staffer stole more than 100 confidential files about an unreleased device and briefed senior Apple leadership on those plans before joining the iPhone maker. Apple denies these allegations, stating it found no evidence of such files on its systems. The legal conflict arrives as OpenAI prepares for a targeted $1.4T IPO valuation and the launch of a smart speaker priced above $300.

selectedTweets.text:
Judge Edward Davila ordered OpenAI to hand Apple its interview files on ex-Apple hardware recruits within 14 days.

The October 13 order partly grants Apple’s bid for early evidence in the trade secrets suit Apple filed on July 10.

OpenAI must produce interview material it has already collected within 5 days and the remaining records within 14 days, including checklists, guides, scripts and technical presentations. 

Those records could show whether interviews touched on Apple technology or components, which sits at the center of Apple’s allegation that OpenAI asked Apple candidates to share secret project details and bring prototypes and components to interviews. 

Davila also ordered forensic device images because he saw a real risk that evidence could be destroyed, citing a conversation between Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng about wiping their Apple-owned devices. 

The judge refused to rush OpenAI’s research on metal finishes, power management and battery functionality, leaving it to the ordinary discovery schedule. 
None of this decides whether secrets were taken, and OpenAI has denied wrongdoing. 

Still, interview files showing Apple parts on the table would tie any misappropriation to OpenAI’s hiring process itself, strengthening Apple’s preliminary injunction motion.
selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
Bloomberg: Apple wants a federal judge to bar OpenAI from using hardware secrets it says former employees carried over.

US District Judge Edward Davila in San Jose hears that injunction request alongside OpenAI’s motion to dismiss the lawsuit.

This is the lawsuit’s first major hearing since Apple sued in July.

Apple says Liu, who joined OpenAI in January, exploited an authentication bug to reach Apple’s network storage and download confidential files. 

Apple’s later filings say he simulated a downloaded power converter schematic in LTspice and told a colleague his AI agent could adjust the circuit itself. 

Apple also claims OpenAI told job candidates to bring prototypes and other “design artifacts” for “show and tell” interview sessions.

An injunction would land as OpenAI readies a smart speaker priced above $300 and an IPO at a targeted $1.4T valuation.

Apple’s hardest task is tracing a specific file from Liu’s downloads into OpenAI’s actual product work.

selectedTweets.text:
All of these incidents, when put together, paint an alarming picture, stoking a suspicion I have, which is, that these companies lack basic operational controls, forget cyber security. 

I would not be surprised if after they IPO we learn that they also lack basic financial checks and balances and are likely not compliant in any cybersecurity, financial or probably even any other framework which govern, specifically, how organizations should handle different areas of their business. 

Part of this pattern is that they find out about these glaring gaps in various compliance areas after someone acts irresponsibly which proves that they also do not have any oversight into various areas of their business.

As I have been saying and will continue to say, the problem here is the culture. It's also the arrogance and the God complex but it's mostly the culture. 

I do not think that these people have ever heard of maturity, either in terms of emotional maturity or maturity in compliance objectives.

I think they had an idea and ran with it. 

There have been reports this week particularly coming out of Meta, which is not a juvenile organization by any stretch, that they didn't even have a plan regarding their models or how to make money with them but it was full steam ahead anyway.

I get living on the edge, I get taking risks and I have no problem with that if the risks you are taking only or going to affect you. 

The risks these companies are taking are affecting everyone who had no say in it and the backlash from the public about these products is quite deafening but is being ignored. 

I mean it's painfully obvious that if the majority of your users are not paying you for your product they obviously do not see any value in it. 

So why you would allow each employee to have $100,000 a month token spend in light of this evidence, is just astonishing.

These are not savvy business leaders and shouldn't be making any decisions which could affect anyone outside of their orbit who is there voluntarily.

But they are and I'm confused why no one in higher positions of power aren't stopping them. In fact it seems that the powers that be are more interested in coddling them then putting them in their place. 

I wouldn't be surprised if you could walk right up to their businesses and walk through a back door because they aren't locked. 

I do not recommend anyone do that as that would be a crime but I'm using that example to illustrate that they just don't know what's going on inside of their companies. 

So when they say they don't know how their products work, I don't think they're being vague to protect their intellectual property so much as they just didn't take the time to learn. 

As I've said imagine Steve Jobs when he was introducing the iPhone getting up on stage and saying here's this thing but I don't know how to work it and I really don't know the inner workings of it but I want you to give me $2,000 for it. 

Just crazy. 

So I think we should believe them. 

They don't know how their product works. 

I don't think they should have the ability to affect anybody else's life until they fully understand it and can explain it. 

But they can't even explain why their employees keep acting out in bizarre ways risking their livelihoods so I wouldn't hold out hope.
